w: Wedged half inside a limestone cliff above the Lokva stream, the current Renaissance castle was built in 1570 on 13th-century foundations. Its most famous owner, robber baron Erazem Predjamski, held off an imperial siege for over a year, using a hidden tunnel through the cave behind him to smuggle in fresh food and taunt his besiegers.
s: A castle built into the mouth of a cliff cave
why: One of the only castles in the world built directly into a cave mouth, with secret tunnels behind it.

w: Built around 1140 on a crag above the Danube, this fortress held Richard the Lionheart captive in 1192 after Duke Leopold V seized him returning in disguise from the Third Crusade. Blown up by Swedish troops in 1645, only broken towers and curtain walls remain, framing the terraced vineyards and river bend far below.
s: Cliff ruin where Richard the Lionheart was jailed
why: The ruin where King Richard the Lionheart was held for ransom, inspiring the legend of his minstrel Blondel.

w: A 15th-century L-plan tower house set within the earthworks of an Iron Age fort above the River Fiddich, Auchindoun was held by the Ogilvies and burned by Clan Mackintosh in 1592 in revenge for the Battle of Glenlivet. No road reaches it; visitors walk across open farmland to the roofless, wind-scoured shell.
s: Remote ruined tower above the River Fiddich
why: A little-visited Highland ruin standing inside the ramparts of a much older Iron Age hillfort.

w: Raised around 1210 by Llywelyn the Great on a rocky knoll in the Lledr valley, this small keep guarded the old route through Snowdonia and is traditionally said to be his birthplace. Edward I's forces captured it in 1283 during the conquest of Wales; a single restored tower now looks out over the surrounding peaks.
s: Llywelyn the Great's mountain stronghold
why: The mountain keep of the Welsh prince who briefly united Wales against English conquest.

w: Randle Wilbraham built this deliberate ruin in 1754 as a summerhouse and eye-catcher on the gritstone ridge straddling the Cheshire-Staffordshire border, arranging tumbled stone and a broken arch to mimic a genuine Norman castle. It became the birthplace of Primitive Methodism after an open-air prayer meeting held here in 1807.
s: A sham ruin built as a folly in 1754
why: A folly built to look ruined from the start, later the site of a founding Methodist camp meeting.

w: First raised as a medieval royal fortress, Borgholm was rebuilt in the 1650s into a lavish Baroque palace for the Swedish nobility, only to burn to a shell in 1806 after soldiers billeted there lit careless fires. The roofless limestone walls, still Sweden's largest castle ruin, stand starkly over Oland's open meadows.
s: Sweden's largest castle ruin, gutted by fire
why: Sweden's largest surviving castle ruin, abandoned after an accidental fire two centuries ago.

w: Built in the 13th century to guard the border between Hungary and Moravia, Cachtice Castle is best known as the residence of Countess Elizabeth Bathory, who was walled into a room here in 1610 after being accused of torturing and murdering servant girls. Abandoned after an 18th-century fire, its broken walls crown a steep wooded hill.
s: Ruined castle tied to the Blood Countess
why: The hilltop ruin where the notorious Countess Bathory was imprisoned until her death.

w: Roman legionaries first fortified this outcrop of towering red sandstone rocks in the 1st century, and the Bulgarians and later the Ottomans expanded it into a full stronghold by the 1830s, weaving stone walls between the natural pillars rather than around them. The result reads as much like a rock formation as a fortress.
s: A fort built into red sandstone rock pillars
why: A fortress built directly into and around a formation of dramatic natural sandstone pillars.

w: Occupying a rocky ridge above the confluence of three rivers, Rozafa's ramparts were rebuilt in turn by Illyrians, Venetians and Ottomans over the site's long life as a stronghold, with most surviving stonework Venetian. Legend holds a woman named Rozafa was walled alive into the foundations so the castle would stand; her handprint is still shown to visitors.
s: Hilltop ruin wrapped in a walling legend
why: A ruin with a grim foundation legend, rebuilt in turn by Illyrians, Venetians and Ottomans.

w: First recorded in the 10th century as Duo Castra, two hillforts, Dvigrad grew into a walled Istrian town of over a thousand people before plague and malaria emptied it by the 1700s. Its Romanesque church, streets and crumbling houses now stand roofless and silent, swallowed by oak woodland with barely another visitor in sight.
s: A whole medieval town abandoned to the forest
why: An entire medieval Istrian town, not just a castle, left to decay after plague emptied it.

w: Built from the 16th to 17th centuries as the seat of the Eristavi dukes guarding the Georgian Military Highway into the mountains, Ananuri's stone towers and two carved churches overlook the turquoise waters of the Zhinvali reservoir. The complex was burned during a bloody 1739 feud between rival branches of the ruling family.
s: Fortress-church complex above a turquoise reservoir
why: A working fortress-church complex above a reservoir, scene of a deadly 18th-century family feud.

w: Perched at 2,300 metres on the slopes of Mount Aragats where two ravines meet, Amberd began as a 7th-century stronghold before the Pahlavuni princes fortified it further in the 11th century and added a domed basilica. Mongol raiders destroyed it in the 13th century, leaving weathered black-stone walls against a backdrop of snow.
s: A fortress-cathedral clinging to Mount Aragats
why: A fortified church complex at 2,300 metres, ruined by Mongol invasion in the 13th century.

w: Two clusters of stone battle and residential towers rise from separate rocky spurs above the Gulikhi gorge, linked in legend by an underground tunnel and once connected visually so defenders could signal danger along the whole Assa valley. Built by Vainakh clans mainly between the 11th and 17th centuries, they remain remarkably intact.
s: Battle towers perched on twin rock spires
why: A rare, near-intact medieval tower settlement built onto two natural rock spurs in the Caucasus.

w: Built from dark local basalt on a Roman fort site occupied since the 3rd century, this stronghold at the Azraq oasis was rebuilt by Ayyubid and Mamluk rulers and later served as T. E. Lawrence's winter headquarters in 1917 during the Arab Revolt. Its heavy stone door, a single carved slab, still swings on its original pivots.
s: Black basalt fort astride an oasis trade route
why: A basalt desert fort that served as T. E. Lawrence's headquarters during the Arab Revolt.

w: Set beside a natural rock-dammed lake far out in Jordan's eastern basalt desert, Qasr Burqu began as a Roman watch post before a Ghassanid Arab building phase and later an Umayyad inscription dated to 700 CE were added to its walls. Reaching it still means hours of empty desert track, with almost no other visitors.
s: An isolated basalt outpost deep in the desert
why: One of Jordan's remotest desert forts, reused across Roman, Ghassanid and Umayyad periods.

w: Garrisoned from the 3rd to 7th centuries to guard the Persian frontier, Zerzevan's above-ground walls hide a warren of rock-cut chambers, grain stores and a rare underground Mithraic temple carved for a secretive Roman soldiers' cult. Excavation only began in earnest in 2014, and much of the site remains underground and unseen.
s: A Roman garrison town hidden underground
why: A Roman frontier fortress hiding an underground Mithraic temple, only excavated since 2014.

w: Built without mortar from precisely shaped granite blocks between the 11th and 15th centuries, Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a Shona kingdom that controlled trade in gold and ivory across the region, its conical tower and curved enclosure walls among the largest ancient structures in sub-Saharan Africa. The modern country later took its name from these ruins.
s: Dry-stone city that gave a nation its name
why: The largest ancient stone city in sub-Saharan Africa, built entirely without mortar.

w: Seat of the Glaoui clan, Berber warlords who controlled the Tizi n'Tichka pass and grew fabulously wealthy under French colonial rule, this kasbah was rebuilt through the early 20th century with elaborate carved cedar and zellige tilework. Abandoned after Moroccan independence in 1956, its painted reception rooms now stand open to the sky.
s: The crumbling seat of the Glaoui warlords
why: The half-collapsed palace of the warlord clan that once controlled the road to the Sahara.

w: Built by Bhati Rajput rulers on a rocky outcrop overlooking the Thar desert, Khaba Fort once anchored a prosperous Paliwal Brahmin village of some eighty settlements. Local legend holds the entire population vanished overnight around 1825 rather than submit to a tyrannical minister's demands, leaving crumbling havelis scattered below the ramparts.
s: A desert fort deserted overnight, legend says
why: A desert fort beside a village whose entire population is said to have vanished overnight.

w: Founded in 1613 by Raja Madho Singh in the Aravalli hills, Bhangarh once housed ten thousand people across temples, havelis and bazaars before being abandoned by the late 18th century for reasons still disputed by historians. The Archaeological Survey of India now bars visitors after dark, feeding its reputation as the country's most haunted ruin.
s: India's most notorious haunted ruin
why: A once-thriving Rajput town abandoned for unclear reasons, now barred to visitors after dark.

w: Rising nearly a hundred metres from the surrounding plain, this granite outcrop became Sri Lanka's capital for barely two decades from 1272, after King Bhuvanekabahu I fled here with the sacred Tooth Relic during South Indian invasions. An ornate stone stairway and carved gateway survive near the summit, though the palace above was later destroyed.
s: A brief 13th-century capital atop a granite rock
why: A short-lived 13th-century royal capital built to defend Buddhism's holiest relic.

w: Raised in 1597 by the daimyo Konishi Yukinaga during Hideyoshi's invasion of Korea, this coastal stronghold used Japanese-style stone-and-earth ramparts unlike any native Korean fortress. It was besieged that winter by combined Korean and Chinese forces under Admiral Yi Sun-sin, whose fleet nearly trapped the garrison before Konishi escaped by sea.
s: A Japanese invasion fort on a Korean coast
why: A rare Japanese-built castle on Korean soil, besieged by the legendary Admiral Yi Sun-sin.

w: Built in just six months in 1591-92 on a headland of the Higashimatsuura Peninsula, Nagoya Castle briefly became Japan's second-largest castle and a city of over a hundred thousand as Toyotomi Hideyoshi massed troops here for his invasions of Korea. Deliberately dismantled after his death, only weathered stone foundations and moats remain among rice fields.
s: Hideyoshi's staging fort for invading Korea
why: The staging base for Hideyoshi's Korean invasions, once briefly Japan's second-largest castle.

w: For a brief span in the 10th century, King Jayavarman IV made Koh Ker the Khmer capital instead of Angkor, raising the seven-tiered sandstone pyramid of Prasat Thom as his state temple. Abandoned when the capital returned to Angkor decades later, dozens of its shrines still lie half-swallowed by jungle far from the main tourist routes.
s: A jungle pyramid built for a rebel Khmer king
why: A short-lived rival capital to Angkor, centred on a striking stepped sandstone pyramid.

w: Ringed by a defensive wall up to nineteen metres high, Kuelap was built from the 6th century onward by the Chachapoya, the pre-Inca 'Warriors of the Clouds,' atop a limestone ridge 3,000 metres up in the northern Andes. Over five hundred circular stone houses once stood inside, later absorbed into the Inca empire shortly before the Spanish conquest.
s: A cloud-forest citadel of the Warriors of the Clouds
why: A vast pre-Inca cloud-forest fortress built by the little-known Chachapoya culture.

w: Named for the twin rock horns crowning its ridge, Waqrapukara was built by the Inca on a sheer promontory above the Apurimac canyon, combining defensive terraces with what researchers believe was a solar observatory and ceremonial platforms. Reachable only by a long mountain trek, it was declared a national heritage site as recently as 2017.
s: A horn-shaped Inca fortress above a canyon
why: A horn-topped Inca ceremonial fortress only granted heritage protection in 2017.

w: Ordered built in 1805 by King Henri Christophe after Haiti won independence from France, this mountaintop citadel rises over 130 metres above its 900-metre peak and was designed to withstand any future French invasion, its walls up to four metres thick. Thousands of formerly enslaved labourers died constructing it; it was never once attacked.
s: The largest fortress in the Americas
why: The largest fortress in the Americas, built by a former slave who crowned himself king.

w: Perched on a bluff at the mouth of the Chagres River, this Spanish fort guarded the river route used to carry Peruvian silver overland to the Caribbean coast. Built in stone from 1595 after an earlier wooden fort burned, it was stormed by the pirate Henry Morgan in 1670 as a prelude to his sack of Panama City, and never fully recovered its old importance.
s: A cliff-edge fort guarding Spain's silver route
why: The fort captured by pirate Henry Morgan before his infamous sack of Panama City.
